I will keep my land in the usual wheat-maize rotation. In Quzhou County, that is the safest way for me to protect income and use the growing season well. I already know how to manage these two crops, the local fields and water conditions fit them, and the buyers are steady. At my age, I do not want to gamble on a crop that needs more market chasing or more delicate management. I will finish the winter wheat that is already in the field, then after harvest I will quickly sow summer maize on the same land so I do not lose time or moisture.

For winter wheat, I will stay with improved seed rather than traditional seed, because I want steadier emergence, stronger disease resistance, and more reliable yield. I will not push fertilizer too hard, but I will feed enough nitrogen to support tillering and grain filling, with phosphorus and potassium as a base so the plants stand better and root better. I will use rotary tillage for the wheat ground because it is practical for me and fits my machinery. I will irrigate about three times if water allows: one at jointing, one around booting or heading, and one at grain filling depending on moisture. I will spray a few times only when needed, mainly for weeds early and then for disease or insects if pressure shows up.

After wheat harvest, I will put the same land straight into summer maize. I will use hybrid maize because that gives me the best yield chance and better stand uniformity. I will keep fertilizer balanced but give maize more nitrogen than wheat, because maize pulls harder during fast vegetative growth and ear filling. I will use rotary tillage again after wheat harvest so I can turn the season quickly. I will irrigate fewer times for maize, mainly watching rainfall, and I will control weeds and corn borers with limited but timely sprays. My goal is not the highest possible yield on paper. My goal is a stable crop, manageable labor, and dependable grain from land I know well.
